smart.SM00442: Acidic and basic fibroblast growth factor family.

description.text: Fibroblast growth factors (FGFs) [[cite:PUB00000068], [cite:PUB00005334]] are a family of multifunctional proteins, often referred to as 'promiscuous growth factors' due to their diverse actions on multiple cell types [[cite:PUB00067626], [cite:PUB00067627]]. FGFs are mitogens, which stimulate growth or differentiation of cells of mesodermal or neuroectodermal origin. The function of FGFs in developmental processes include mesoderm induction, anterior-posterior patterning, limb development, and neural induction and development. In mature tissues, they are involved in diverse processes including keratinocyte organisation and wound healing [[cite:PUB00021048], [cite:PUB00067628], [cite:PUB00067629], [cite:PUB00067630], [cite:PUB00067631], [cite:PUB00067632]]. FGF involvement is critical during normal development of both vertebrates and invertebrates, and irregularities in their function leads to a range of developmental defects [[cite:PUB00067633], [cite:PUB00067634], [cite:PUB00067635], [cite:PUB00067636]]. Fibroblast growth factors are heparin-binding proteins and interactions with cell-surface-associated heparan sulfate proteoglycans have been shown to be essential for FGF signal transduction. FGFs have internal pseudo-threefold symmetry (β-trefoil topology) [[cite:PUB00024683]]. There are currently over 20 different FGF family members that have been identified in mammals, all of which are structurally related signaling molecules [[cite:PUB00039267], [cite:PUB00021048]]. They exert their effects through four distinct membrane fibroblast growth factor receptors (FGFRs), FGFR1 to FGFR4 [[cite:PUB00001036]], which belong to the tyrosine kinase superfamily. Upon binding to FGF, the receptors dimerize and their intracellular tyrosine kinase domains become active [[cite:PUB00001036]].
